title: Present Simple
subtitle: Things we do every day
goals: I can say what people do every day.
I can use plays, watches, has … with he, she and it.
I can say don't and doesn't.
I can ask Do …? and Does …? and answer Yes / No.

learn.title: Every day
learn.rule: We use these sentences for things we do again and again.

examples.text: I get up at seven **every day**.
examples.speaker: Sam

practice.prompt: Look at the days. Sam drinks water ___.
Look at the days. Sam plays football ___.

learn.teacherNote: Meaning first: things we do again and again. The ticks in the week strip show “every day”. One picture alone does not prove “every day”, so use the calendar.

learn.title: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
learn.rule: One: I, you, he, she, it. Two or more: we, they.

examples.speaker: Mia
examples.label: you = Sam. Mia is talking to Sam.

examples.speaker: Mia
examples.label: we = Mia + Sam. Mia is talking.

learn.teacherNote: For I and you, look at the speech bubble: the speaker says “I”; the person they talk to is “you”. Count on fingers: one person (he / she / it) or two or more (we / they).

learn.title: I / you / we / they + play
learn.rule: With I, you, we and they, use play.
learn.teacherNote: The verb does not change with I, you, we and they. Chant it: “I play, you play, we play, they play.”

learn.title: He / she / it + plays
learn.rule: Use plays with he, she and it.
learn.teacherNote: When the subject changes, the verb changes: I play → He plays. Names (Mia, Sam) work like he / she. brush my teeth → She brushes her teeth: the possessive changes too.

learn.title: plays, watches, goes, studies, has
learn.rule: Look at the end of the word.
learn.teacherNote: All forms come from a checked list, not from adding letters blindly. play → plays (vowel before y), study → studies (consonant before y). have → has is special.

learn.title: I / you / we / they + don't
learn.rule: I, you, we, they + don't + play.

examples.text: We **don't** watch TV in the morning.
examples.speaker: Sam

examples.text: They **don't** go to school on Sunday.
They do not play. = They **don't** play.
examples.label: do not = don't

practice.prompt: We ___ watch TV in the morning.
practice.explain: We don't watch TV in the morning.

learn.teacherNote: don't = do not. After don't the verb stays in its base form.

learn.title: He / she / it + doesn't
learn.rule: He, she, it + doesn't + play. After doesn't, use play.

examples.label: doesn't = helper word. do = the action.

learn.teacherNote: “Does comes, the verb goes back”: plays → play, has → have, studies → study. It is not only “take away the s”. In “He doesn't do his homework.” doesn't is the helper and do is the action.

learn.title: Do you …?
learn.rule: Start with Do: Do you play football?

examples.text: **Do** you brush your teeth every morning?
examples.speaker: Ms. Rosa
examples.label: my → your

learn.teacherNote: Do questions go with I / you / we / they. With “you”, use “your”: Do you brush your teeth?

learn.title: Does he …?
learn.rule: Start with Does. Then use play.
learn.teacherNote: When Does comes first, the main verb is in base form: Does he play? Does she have? Does Mia study?

learn.title: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
learn.rule: Does she play? Yes, she does. No, she doesn't.

examples.q: Do you watch TV in the morning?
Do you and Sam study English?
examples.label: you and Sam → we

practice.prompt: Ms. Rosa asks Sam: “Do you play football?” Sam plays football. Sam says:
practice.explain: Sam talks about Sam: Yes, I do.

learn.teacherNote: Keep the speaker in short answers: the teacher asks “Do you …?”, the pupil says “Yes, I do.” Personal questions can have Yes or No — both are right.

learn.title: What? Where? What time?
learn.rule: What / Where / What time + do / does + …?

practice.explain: What time does Sam get up?

learn.teacherNote: Keep WH questions short and supported. Not every English question starts with Do / Does; this week looks at questions with action verbs. Times are shown as clocks on screen.

practice.prompt: He reads. Which is the question?
They eat apples. Which is the negative?

learn.teacherNote: Positive, negative and question side by side with the same meaning. The last example shows “She is happy.” vs “She plays.”: is-sentences do not use do / does. Keep it short — to be is not this week's topic.

learn.title: Book words: live, ride, dance …
learn.rule: These are action words. With he, she and it, add s.
learn.teacherNote: Target words from the coursebook page (live, speak, study, dance, play, walk, ride, eat, smile, visit). dance → dances and ride → rides only add s (the e is already there). Ask: Where do you live? What do you do?

examples.text: Ana ride**s** a bike to school.
examples.label: ride → rides

practice.explain: Ana rides a bike to school.

teacherGoals: Present Simple with action verbs for habits.
I / you / we / they vs he / she / it; -s, -es, -ies and has.
Do / Does yes-no questions and short answers; supported What / Where / What time.
teacherNote: This module is about sentences with action verbs (play, read, have…). am / is / are are not this week's topic; Learn 12 only shows the short difference between “She is happy.” and “She plays.” This version is not linked to a textbook; it uses general beginner everyday words.
